params.title: MF-HF-DSC-SITOR (NBDP) Equip. & Ops
params.subtitle: MF and HF frequencies and controls, how SSB, DSC and SITOR (NBDP) signals work, and how to diagnose receiver and transmitter faults.

scenes.narration: This lesson covers the GMDSS, or Global Maritime Distress and Safety System, equipment that works in the medium frequency and high frequency bands, MF and HF for short. We'll learn the frequencies and bandwidths, the transceiver's controls, and how single sideband, or SSB, digital selective calling, or DSC, and SITOR signals are generated, received and exchanged. SITOR, simplex teletype over radio, is also called NBDP, narrow-band direct printing. Then we'll diagnose receiver and transmitter faults from their symptoms and meter readings. First up: frequencies and bandwidth.

onScreen: J3E SSB voice: 2.8 kHz bandwidth, 3.0 kHz spacing
J2B SITOR (NBDP): 300 Hz bandwidth, 500 Hz spacing
170 Hz FSK at 100 baud needs only about 300 Hz
scenes.narration: Every signal type has an assigned bandwidth and a channel spacing. J3E is single-sideband voice. Its assigned bandwidth is 2.8 kilohertz, which is why the emission is written 2K80J3E, and its channel spacing is 3.0 kilohertz. J2B is SITOR, or NBDP. Its assigned bandwidth is only 300 hertz, with a channel spacing of 500 hertz. Why so narrow? NBDP uses frequency-shift keying, or FSK, with a 170 hertz shift at 100 baud, and that needs only about 300 hertz.

params.title: Frequency tolerance: 10 Hz
steps: Other pairs: 9 or 10 Hz off, at or near the limit
Flag: a 2 ppm counter may be off ≈4.4 or 8.3 Hz

scenes.narration: The allowable frequency tolerance for GMDSS MF-HF transmitters is 10 hertz. That's tight enough for narrow, 170 hertz shift DSC and NBDP signals to land in the receiver's narrow filters. The exam checks this with a frequency counter accurate to 2 parts per million, or 2 ppm. A reading of 2182.006 kilohertz is 6 hertz high. A reading of 4124.995 kilohertz is 5 hertz low. Every other pair includes an offset of 9 or 10 hertz, at or near the limit. A flag note: a 2 ppm counter can itself be off by about 4.4 hertz at 2182 kilohertz and 8.3 hertz at 4125 kilohertz, so no pair is provably legal. For the exam, choose 2182.006 and 4124.995 kilohertz: the smallest offsets.

params.title: DSC and follow-on frequencies
items: Exam sets: voice 4125, 8291, 16420 kHz · NBDP 2174.5, 6268, 12520 kHz
DSC frequencies are not follow-on channels; follow-on frequencies are not DSC

onScreen: Keep DSC and follow-on lists apart
scenes.narration: Now the frequencies. Each band from 2 to 16 megahertz has a DSC frequency, with voice and NBDP follow-on frequencies beside it. The 6 DSC frequencies are 2187.5, 4207.5, 6312, 8414.5, 12577 and 16804.5 kilohertz. Voice follow-on uses 2182, 4125, 6215, 8291, 12290 and 16420 kilohertz. NBDP follow-on uses 2174.5, 4177.5, 6268, 8376.5, 12520 and 16695 kilohertz. The exam's voice set is 4125, 8291 and 16420. Its NBDP set is 2174.5, 6268 and 12520. Keep the lists apart: DSC frequencies such as 6312 and 8414.5 are not follow-on channels, and follow-on frequencies such as 2182, 4125, 4177.5, 8291, 8376.5 and 12520 are not DSC frequencies.

callouts.label: R.I.T. (clarifier): slight changes to the receive frequency only
TLX on the display: operating in SITOR (NBDP)
ENTER: accepts the previous selection or data input
Distress alerts: a separate, covered button

onScreen: R.I.T.: adjusts receive frequency, transmit stays put
scenes.narration: Here's the MF-HF transceiver console. The R.I.T. control, for receiver incremental tuning, is also called the clarifier. It makes slight adjustments in the receiver frequency, while the transmit frequency stays on the assigned channel. When the display shows TLX, for telex, the transceiver is operating in SITOR, or NBDP. The ENTER function accepts the previous selection or data input, such as a frequency or an MMSI, a Maritime Mobile Service Identity. Distress alerts don't go through ENTER: they use a separate, covered button.

onScreen: Coupler adjusts its matching network to 50 Ω
Antenna tuned to the transmit frequency
scenes.narration: Next, the TUNE button. Pressing TUNE tunes the antenna to the transmit frequency. The transmitter usually sends a low-power carrier while the automatic antenna coupler adjusts its matching network, until the antenna matches the transmitter's 50 ohm output.

params.title: RF Gain and AGC
rows: Stops strong nearby signals or noise overloading
Cuts gain on strong signals, raises it on weak

onScreen: RF Gain down: less RF amplifier sensitivity
Helps with strong nearby signals or heavy noise
Less gain on strong signals, more on weak
scenes.narration: 2 gain controls. Reducing the RF Gain control reduces the sensitivity of the radio frequency, or RF, amplifier stage. That helps when strong nearby signals or heavy noise would overload the receiver. AGC, automatic gain control, works on its own. It maintains a relatively constant audio frequency, or AF, output when the input signal varies, by cutting the gain on strong signals and raising it on weak ones.

blocks.label: Noise blanker
blocks.note: Gates the I.F. off for each spike

onScreen: RF amplifier, high first I.F., low second I.F., product detector
High first I.F.: eliminates image signals
Low second I.F.: sharp selectivity and gain
Noise blanker gates off the I.F. amplifier for each spike
scenes.narration: Inside the receiver, the signal passes the RF amplifier, then a high first I.F., or intermediate frequency, then a low second I.F., and on to the product detector. Why a high first I.F.? Its primary purpose is eliminating image signals. An image lies twice the I.F. away from the wanted signal, so with a high I.F. it falls far outside the front-end passband. The low second I.F. then supplies sharp selectivity and gain. Against noise spikes, a noise blanker uses the noise pulses themselves to develop a blanking pulse that briefly gates off the I.F. amplifier for the length of each spike. It doesn't clip peaks or reduce RF gain. Last, the beat frequency oscillator, or BFO, feeds the detector.

params.title: The BFO restores the carrier
labels: J3E: carrier suppressed, a single sideband sent
The BFO re-injects the carrier frequency at the detector
It does not recreate the missing sideband
Garbled voice: adjust R.I.T. or Clarifier, not squelch

onScreen: BFO re-injects the carrier at the detector
scenes.narration: J3E suppresses the carrier and sends a single sideband. To demodulate it, the BFO re-injects the carrier frequency in the receiver's detector. Note what the BFO does not do: it does not recreate the missing sideband. And if another vessel's HF transmission sounds garbled, use the R.I.T. or Clarifier control to adjust the receiver frequency until the voice sounds natural. Don't reach for squelch: it only mutes or unmutes the audio.

params.title: With the BFO turned off
rows: Still received: carries its own carrier
Still received: carries its own carrier

onScreen: J2B, A1A, F1B: need the BFO
scenes.narration: What if the BFO is turned off? A3E, double-sideband amplitude modulation, and H3E, single sideband with full carrier, can still be received, because they carry their own carrier. J3E needs the BFO, and so do J2B, A1A and F1B. So with the BFO off, you'll still hear A3E and H3E, but not the others.

badges.label: Attack
badges.note: Gain drops instantly on voice peaks

badges.label: Decay
badges.note: Noise doesn't surge up between words

onScreen: Fast attack: gain drops instantly on peaks
Slow decay: no noise surge between words
scenes.narration: One more receiver setting the exam asks about. An AGC circuit for SSB voice reception should have fast attack and slow decay. Fast attack means the gain drops instantly when a voice peak arrives. Slow decay means the gain recovers gently, so the noise doesn't surge up in the gaps between words.

onScreen: Voice but no NBDP: 500 Hz filter
NBDP but no voice: 2.8 kHz filter
scenes.narration: The receiver has 2 I.F. filter paths. Voice and SSB go through a 2.8 kilohertz filter. SITOR, or NBDP, goes through a narrow 500 hertz I.F. filter. So if you hear signals in voice or SSB mode but not in NBDP mode, suspect a defective 500 hertz I.F. filter: it's the narrow path only NBDP uses. Now flip it. If you hear signals in NBDP mode but not in voice or SSB mode, suspect a defective 2.8 kilohertz filter, the wider path only voice uses.

params.title: Receiver symptoms and causes
rows: Garbled voice on all SSB channels
One very high-pitched voice; all else normal
That station's transmitter is off frequency
Inoperative VCO, part of the loop
Failed variable gain amplifier in the RF stage

onScreen: One high-pitched voice: that transmitter off frequency
No AGC: variable gain amplifier in the RF stage
scenes.narration: 4 more symptoms. Garbled, unreadable voice on all MF-HF SSB channels most likely means the BFO circuit has failed. SSB is intelligible only when the BFO reinserts the carrier at the correct frequency. But if all signals sound normal except one very high-pitched, barely readable voice, that station's transmitter is off frequency. Your receiver's BFO, synthesizer and voltage controlled oscillator, or VCO, are clearly working. A phase locked loop, or PLL, that appears faulty is most likely caused by an inoperative VCO, which is part of the loop itself. And an inoperative AGC function is most likely caused by failure of a variable gain amplifier in the RF stage: the amplifier the AGC control voltage acts on.

params.title: No signals? Work out to the antenna

blocks.label: Dummy load
blocks.note: Connected in place of the antenna

onScreen: Strong AF, no signals: no antenna signal reaches the receiver
Open circuit in the transmission line
Signal breaks up, meter mid scale to 0: intermittent antenna-coupler link
Or connected to a dummy load
scenes.narration: Now work outward from the receiver. Suppose it gives strong AF output, but you hear no signals on any frequency. No antenna signal is reaching it. One cause is an open circuit in the transmission line to the antenna. A different symptom: the signal breaks up while the Signal meter alternates between mid scale and 0. That points to an intermittent connection between the antenna and the coupler. The Signal meter reads RF strength ahead of the audio stages, so the fault is out in the antenna circuit. And back to strong AF with no signals: the other cause is a transceiver connected to a dummy load instead of the antenna.

callouts.label: AF not suppressed without a strong enough signal: squelch failed
No AF, speaker leads read near 0 Ω: audio amplifier stage failed
TX lamp lit, powered on, no AF output
Shorted Push-To-Talk circuit holds the set in transmit

onScreen: AF not suppressed with no signal: squelch failed
No AF, speaker reads near 0 Ω: audio amplifier failed
scenes.narration: Now the audio end. If the receiver fails to suppress the AF output in the absence of a sufficiently strong input signal, the squelch circuit has failed. If there's no AF output, check between the speaker leads with an ohmmeter. A speaker voice coil normally measures only a few ohms, so a reading near 0 ohms means the speaker is fine and the audio amplifier stage has failed. Last, no AF output while the radio is powered on and TX, the transmit indicator, is illuminated. That points to a shorted Push-To-Talk circuit in the microphone. It holds the set in transmit, which mutes the receiver.

onScreen: Double balanced mixer cancels the carrier
scenes.narration: How is a J3E signal generated? Audio from the microphone goes into a double balanced mixer, which cancels the carrier and leaves 2 sidebands. Then a sideband filter removes one sideband, giving J3E. The carrier oscillator feeds the mixer, but its carrier never comes out. Which sideband goes? The lower sideband is eliminated by a filter that passes the upper sideband and blocks the lower, because marine MF-HF radiotelephony uses upper sideband. And for initial MF-HF communications, the most likely power level is 150 watts P E P, peak envelope power, raised only if the other station has trouble copying.

marks.label: 1700 Hz offset
marks.note: From the carrier frequency: a 170 Hz shift

onScreen: 1700 ± 85 Hz from the carrier: 170 Hz shift
scenes.narration: Shipboard GMDSS equipment most commonly generates SITOR, or NBDP, by feeding audio tones into the SSB transmitter. The result is 2 alternating sidebands of 1615 hertz and 1785 hertz, offset from the carrier frequency by 1700 hertz. That's 1700 plus or minus 85 hertz: a 170 hertz shift.

onScreen: Phase comparator compares the divided outputs
Error voltage pulls the VCO onto frequency
scenes.narration: Now the phase locked loop frequency synthesizer. It's made up of a master oscillator, frequency dividers, a phase comparator, a loop filter and a voltage controlled oscillator. The master oscillator's output is divided down and fed to the phase comparator. The VCO's output is divided down too. The phase comparator compares the 2 divided outputs and produces an error voltage. Through the loop filter, that voltage pulls the VCO onto frequency.

params.title: 2182 kHz radiotelephone: fault or normal?
items: No contact with a station 60 miles away by day: malfunction
Daytime ground wave normally reaches roughly 100 to 150 nautical miles
No power output indicated when speaking into the microphone: malfunction
Can't reach a shore station 600 nautical miles away by day: normal

onScreen: 60 miles by day, no contact: malfunction
Ground wave: roughly 100 to 150 nautical miles
No power output when speaking: malfunction
scenes.narration: Now transmitter faults, starting with a 2182 kilohertz radiotelephone system. Failure to contact another station 60 miles away during daytime indicates a malfunction, because daytime ground-wave coverage normally reaches roughly 100 to 150 nautical miles. No indication of power output when you speak into the microphone is also a symptom of malfunction in a 2182 kilohertz SSB radiotelephone. But failing to reach a shore station 600 nautical miles away in daytime is normal: that's beyond daytime coverage.

onScreen: Flag: '1615 kHz audio oscillator' means 1615 Hz
Most likely: failed 500 Hz I.F. filter
scenes.narration: Next: an MF-HF transceiver works properly on voice but not on SITOR, or NBDP. Voice goes from the microphone through the SSB exciter to the output, and it's fine. NBDP depends on parts voice never uses. A tone oscillator supplies the 1615 and 1785 hertz tones, and without the 1615 hertz tone the transmitter cannot form the NBDP signal. The 500 hertz I.F. filter is a part only NBDP depends on, and it's the most likely failure. A flag note: the exam also keys 'the 1615 kilohertz audio oscillator is not working' for this same symptom. It means the 1615 hertz tone oscillator. Choose it if you see it.

params.title: Power meter on a 60 W PEP SSB set
rows: Flickers widely, peaks up to 60 W, not above

onScreen: J3E with speech: flickers up to 60 W, not above
ARQ: swings regularly from 0 to 60 W
210 ms block of 3 characters, then a pause
scenes.narration: What does proper operation look like on a 60 watt P E P SSB transmitter's power meter? In J3E, keyed without speaking, there's no power output. With speech, the meter flickers widely with the voice peaks, up to but not above 60 watts, instead of holding steady. In SITOR ARQ, automatic repeat request, the meter fluctuates regularly from 0 to the 60 watt reading. Each 210 millisecond block of 3 characters is followed by a pause while the set listens for the acknowledgement.

badges.label: ARQ: 3-character block
badges.note: Transmitting: meter up to full power

badges.label: ARQ: full cycle with the pause

onScreen: Cycle repeats every 450 ms: 0 to 150 W on a 150 W set
FEC: continuous, steady 225 to 250 W on a 250 W set
scenes.narration: Now the F1B modes. A 150 watt MF-HF transmitter working properly in F1B ARQ mode shows output that fluctuates between 0 and 150 watts. ARQ sends a 210 millisecond block of 3 characters, then pauses for the acknowledgement, repeating every 450 milliseconds. FEC, forward error correction, is different. It sends continuously with a constant-envelope FSK signal, so the meter holds steady. A 250 watt transmitter working properly in F1B FEC mode shows constant output between 225 and 250 watts.

params.title: Proper or improper? F1B power readings

scenes.narration: Put them side by side, because the exam likes to swap the modes. A 0 to 150 watt swing is proper in ARQ. Constant output near rated power is proper in FEC: 225 to 250 watts on a 250 watt set, or 125 to 150 watts on a 150 watt set. But in F1B FEC mode, output that fluctuates between 0 and 150 watts on a 150 watt transmitter indicates improper operation. That swing is normal only for ARQ.

onScreen: High SWR: very low RF output in FEC
Dummy load: matched 50 Ω, full output
scenes.narration: A standing wave ratio, or SWR, meter reads 125 watts forward and 5 watts reflected. Acceptable? First the reflection coefficient, gamma: the square root of 5 over 125, which is 0.2. Then SWR is 1 plus gamma over 1 minus gamma: 1.2 over 0.8, or 1.5 to 1. That's acceptable. A high SWR in the antenna system is a different story. In F1B FEC mode it can cause very low RF output, as the protection circuit cuts power to save the amplifier. A dummy load, by contrast, is a matched 50 ohm termination, so it allows full output.

params.title: No RF output, and valid FEC tests
items: Crowbar circuit activated: DC power to the transmitter shut off, so 0 RF output
Not valid for F1B FEC: spectrum analyzer test of frequency deviation
F1B simply shifts between 2 fixed frequencies 170 Hz apart
Valid: visual inspection and DVM power supply checks
Valid: input/output checks with a 10:1 oscilloscope probe

onScreen: Spectrum analyzer deviation test: not valid
scenes.narration: If the RF output drops to 0, look at the power supply. Activation of a crowbar circuit, which prevents an unregulated voltage increase, shuts off the DC power to the transmitter, so there's 0 RF output. And when hunting an F1B FEC transmitter fault, know which tests are valid. Modulation testing with an RF spectrum analyzer to measure frequency deviation is not valid, because F1B simply shifts between 2 fixed frequencies 170 hertz apart. Valid methods are visual inspection, power supply checks with a DVM, or digital voltmeter, and input and output checks with a 10 to 1 oscilloscope probe.

params.title: Anatomy of a DSC distress alert

badges.label: Dot pattern
badges.note: Alternating dots at 100 baud: scanners stop and synchronize

badges.label: Each message character
badges.note: Time diversity: sent again after 4 other characters

scenes.narration: Now DSC on MF and HF. A DSC distress alert call starts with an alternating dot pattern of 200 bits, which precedes the phasing signal. At 100 baud, those 200 bits last 2 seconds, long enough for scanning watch receivers to stop and synchronize. Then comes the phasing signal, and then the message. Each character is sent again 400 milliseconds later. That's the time diversity reception interval, and 400 milliseconds is a number the exam tests.

params.title: The DSC code and the 400 ms interval
steps: Check bits count the 0 bits in the information
Each character repeats after 4 other characters

onScreen: 4/3 ratio is the 7-bit SITOR code, not DSC
scenes.narration: Here's where 400 milliseconds comes from. DSC uses a 10 bit code: 7 bits used for information and 3 bits used for error correction. Those 3 check bits are a count of the 0 bits in the information part. Don't confuse this with a constant 4 to 3 ratio of 1 bits to 0 bits: that's the 7 bit SITOR code, not DSC. Each character is repeated after 4 other characters. 4 times 10 bits is 40 bits, and at 100 bits per second, that takes 400 milliseconds: the MF-HF-DSC time diversity reception interval.

onScreen: MF/HF DSC: ±85 Hz on a 1700 Hz sub-carrier
scenes.narration: Compare MF-HF DSC with the VHF, or very high frequency, version. MF-HF-DSC uses a frequency shift of plus or minus 85 hertz on a 1700 hertz sub-carrier, giving tones of 1615 and 1785 hertz. The 1300 and 2100 hertz tones belong to VHF DSC. MF-HF DSC runs at 100 baud, VHF DSC at 1200 baud. And the time diversity interval is 400 milliseconds on MF-HF, against 33 and a third milliseconds on VHF.

params.title: Distress calls and MMSI 003669999
items: Distress call: MMSI, position, nature of distress, follow-on by J3E or F1B
DSC identifies ships by MMSI, not by call sign or vessel name
MMSI 003669999: group call for all U.S. Coast Guard coast stations
Received by all DSC-equipped USCG coast stations in range; may auto-acknowledge
May be used to test MF/HF DSC equipment aboard ships

onScreen: Distress call contents: MMSI, position, nature, follow-on mode
OK for testing ship MF/HF DSC
scenes.narration: An MF-HF distress priority DSC call may include the ship's MMSI, its position, the nature of distress, and follow-on communications by J3E voice or F1B telex. DSC identifies ships by MMSI, not by call sign or vessel name. One MMSI to know: 0 0 3 6 6 9 9 9 9. It's the group call for all U.S. Coast Guard coast stations. A call to it is received by all DSC-equipped Coast Guard coast stations within range, which may send an automated acknowledgement. And it may be used to test MF-HF DSC equipment aboard ships.

onScreen: ISS sends a block of 3 characters
NAVTEX and MSI broadcasts: not ARQ
scenes.narration: SITOR ARQ is a two-way exchange. The information sending station, or ISS, transmits a block of 3 characters. The information receiving station, or IRS, checks each block for parity: each character's fixed 4 to 3 bit ratio. If the block is correct, a control signal tells the ISS to proceed. If the parity check fails, the block must be resent. So when a ship works a shore station, the ship sends a group of 3 characters and the shore station checks parity. If parity is OK, the shore station indicates readiness for the next 3 characters, asking for a repeat only when the check fails. Sending each character twice belongs to FEC, not ARQ. And NAVTEX and maritime safety information, or MSI, broadcasts are one-way, so they cannot be contacted or copied in ARQ.

params.title: Direct telex through a coast station

onScreen: Land line to the TELEX subscriber
KKKK ends the direct TELEX connection
scenes.narration: To send a message via a direct connection to a shoreside TELEX subscriber, the ship works the automated coast station in ARQ and sends D I R T L X, followed by the subscriber's telex number and a plus sign. The coast station connects the radio circuit to the subscriber over the land line. When you're done, send K K K K. That terminates the direct TELEX connection, clearing the land-line link, while the radio circuit can stay up.

params.title: Coast station commands
items: Most ARQ commands end with '+': HELP+, MSG+
DIRTLX0xxyyyy+: direct connection to a shoreside TELEX subscriber
MSG+ retrieves waiting messages
AMV+ sends an AMVER report · OPR+ calls the operator
KKKK terminates a direct TELEX connection

scenes.narration: When working an automated coast station, most ARQ commands are followed by a plus sign, as in HELP plus and M S G plus. Here's the set to know. D I R T L X with the subscriber's number and a plus sign asks for a direct TELEX connection. M S G plus retrieves messages waiting for you. A M V plus sends an AMVER report, to the Automated Mutual-assistance Vessel Rescue system. O P R plus calls the operator. And K K K K terminates a direct TELEX connection.

onScreen: SFEC: one-way to a single station
SFEC: receive without transmitting, as under radio silence
scenes.narration: SITOR has 3 modes, and the exam lists them in order: ARQ, FEC, SFEC. ARQ is two-way communications. FEC is one-way communications to all stations. SFEC, selective FEC, is one-way communications to a single station. When would you use SFEC? When an individual station must receive communications without transmitting, as under radio silence.

params.title: FEC: every character sent twice
labels: Mode B: each character sent twice, separated in time
A static crash corrupts one copy
The receiver replaces it with the other copy

onScreen: Mode B FEC: each character sent twice
scenes.narration: In SITOR Mode B, forward error correction reduces the error rate in the presence of static crashes. Each character is transmitted twice, separated in time. If a static crash corrupts one copy, as it does here, the receiver replaces it with the other copy. No reply is needed, so FEC works one-way.

params.title: Receiving MSI on the MF/HF console

marks.label: 518 kHz FEC TELEX
marks.note: In NAVTEX range, NAVTEX and Sat-C both down

marks.label: 4210 kHz
marks.note: Lowest of the 8 HF MSI frequencies

onScreen: In NAVTEX range: 518 kHz FEC TELEX
Beyond range or in the tropics: HF MSI frequency, FEC TELEX
scenes.narration: Now a practical one. You're within range of NAVTEX broadcasts, but both the Inmarsat-C and the NAVTEX receiver are inoperative. Select 518 kilohertz FEC TELEX on the MF-HF console to receive MSI. Not ARQ: ARQ cannot copy a broadcast. Beyond range of NAVTEX with the Sat-C system failed, select an HF MSI frequency and FEC TELEX mode. And when atmospheric interference spoils NAVTEX, especially in the tropics, select one of the 8 HF MSI frequencies, from 4210 to 26100.5 kilohertz, and set up the transceiver in FEC TELEX mode.

callouts.label: Antenna tuner: cancels reactance, transforms impedance to 50 Ω
RG-8, 50 Ω coax; not 72–75 Ω RG-59, RG-6 or RG-179
PL-259 connector; not F (75 Ω TV), SMA (microwave) or EIA-232 (serial)

onScreen: Antenna tuner: matches to 50 Ω, minimizes SWR
scenes.narration: Now the antenna system. The antenna tuner matches the antenna to the operating frequency. It cancels reactance and transforms the impedance to the transmitter's 50 ohms, so SWR is minimized. The feed line is RG-8, 50 ohm coax. 72 to 75 ohm cables such as RG-59, RG-6 and RG-179 would mismatch the system. And the connector you'll often see is the PL-259. F connectors are for 75 ohm TV cable, SMA is a small microwave connector, and EIA-232 is a serial data interface.

onScreen: Series inductance: electrically longer, lower resonant frequency
Series capacitance: electrically shorter, higher resonant frequency
scenes.narration: You can change an antenna's electrical length without changing its physical length. An inductance in series with the antenna electrically lengthens a physically fixed length antenna and lowers its resonant frequency. That's how loading coils let short whips work on MF. A capacitance in series does the opposite: it electrically shortens the antenna and raises its resonant frequency.

params.title: Whip carried away? Rig a wire

blocks.label: 10 ft wire
blocks.note: Too short to tune on MF

onScreen: Rig a 35–40 ft wire per the manual
scenes.narration: Suppose the MF-HF whip antenna is carried away. Don't use the VHF antenna: it is not usable at these frequencies. A 10 foot wire won't do either: it's too short to tune on MF. Instead, rig a wire antenna approximately 35 to 40 feet long, following the equipment instruction manual, and let the antenna tuner match it.
